items.title: Scaling Git for agentic software engineering
items.summary: In a recent engineering blog post, Anthropic described how agentic coding pushed its source control past what Git was designed for: Merges to its monorepo grew from around 2,500 a day in May to more than 30,000 a day by September. Its team built an in-house system, Scion, around the assumption that nearly all clients are agents that are always online.Anthropic is clear that Scion isn't meant to be a replacement for Git and has not been designed with Git compatibility in mind. Instead, it has been aimed at resolving the scaling problems that could become common over the next six to 12 months. The article suggests Git platforms can evolve and implement richer server-side operations, while maintaining Git compatibility. That's the problem space our next-gen source code management (SCM) work is aimed at."Scaling our monorepo for agentic development has changed how we think about Git server architecture. We see room to expand what Git servers can do for these workloads without departing from the overall Git model."Nick G., Source Control, AnthropicGitLab’s next-gen SCM design pairs agent-facing interfaces with a horizontally scalable backend, using the Git protocol to address the same infrastructure pressures.This work supports the DevOps infrastructure layer in GitLab’s broader vision for a governed software factory. At Transcend, our global customer event, GitLab described the factory as a connected system that helps teams move software from idea to production under their own policies and standards. Teams need to trace changes, understand their context, and apply policy as work moves through the software lifecycle.Serving large repositoriesWe use the Git protocol developers and their tools already rely on as the foundation of our next-gen SCM. Its backend can scale across many compute nodes, and its interfaces let agents request the files and history needed for each task. This can reduce repeated full repository clones.The architecture separates compute from repository storage. Object storage holds repository data. Stateless compute nodes serve requests from local caches. You can expand compute resources by adding nodes, and the components communicate through the standard S3 API. You can run it on GitLab.com and self-managed environments, including air-gapped environments where repository data never leaves your infrastructure.This design aims to reduce bottlenecks from heavy read and write activity. In early internal tests, workloads completed up to 50x faster, used half the tokens, and generated up to 1,000x less network traffic.What we’re building nextThe backend is one part of preparing source control for coding agents. You also need to know what instructions shaped a change, which commits and merge requests were affected, and which policies applied. The roadmap includes these capabilities.GitLab plans to capture the instructions and decisions behind an agent session as the work happens, giving teams a record of the context that shaped a change.Each session will remain linked to the commits and merge requests it produces, including after a squash or rebase, so teams can trace agent work to the code it changed.Reviewers will see changes alongside relevant context so they can focus on the work that needs human judgment.Branch policies will apply to agent identities, allowing teams to control which agents can change specific code.These capabilities on the roadmap are designed to give you a clearer record of how agent work was produced, reviewed, and governed. They build on the platform’s orchestration, lifecycle context, governance, and security.Together with the communityScaling improvements in Git helps each client and host, and you don’t have to depend on a fork for your source control. That's why much of our Git work happens upstream. Git remains a collaborative project and GitLab has been the largest corporate contributor to Git in recent releases. Git contributions from many companies and the wider community shape every release, continuously iterating and evolving Git.GitLab delivered a pluggable interface for Git's object storage in Git 2.54 and has been moving more of Git's object database subsystems behind it. And in Git 2.56, consistency checks, housekeeping, and packfile generation moved behind the interface, and that work continues. The interface belongs to the Git project and serves clients as well as servers. GitLab’s next generation of SCM will run as our own fast, scalable implementation of it with agent-facing interfaces. Also, we intend to extend the same abstraction to upstream Git, improving how Git handles large binary files. GitLab will continue working with the Git community on how capabilities like these can serve every Git client.Evaluate next-gen SCM with your own repositoriesYou can request early access to GitLab’s next-gen source code management solution, and test it against the repositories that strain your Git backend today.This blog post contains "forward‑looking statements" with
